definitions.definition: Sparse ensemble pruning: an ensemble reduced to the members that maximise a submodular objective.
The 40 classification data sets of the invented UCI-40 collection.
Each data set split into ten folds, each fold held out once.
Mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and outcomes, averaged over data sets.

claims.statement: The expected loss of the pruned [[D1:SEP]] ensemble is within a factor $1+\epsilon$ of the full ensemble's.

relations.note: Greedy pruning has no guarantee on the loss.

claims.statement: On the [[D3:UCI-40 collection]], [[D2:SEP with 20 members]] has a lower [[D6:Brier score]] than [[D4:random forest]] and gradient boosting, but a lower accuracy than gradient boosting.
The pruning objective of [[D1:SEP]] is monotone submodular.
[[D1:SEP]] predicts four times faster than the full ensemble.
The losses of the ensemble members are bounded in $[0, 1]$.

evidence.description: SEP with 20 members compared with random forest and gradient boosting on the UCI-40 collection by 10-fold cross-validation.

tables.description: Brier score and accuracy of three methods on the UCI-40 collection

limitations.statement: Each data set was run once, so no spread is reported.

references.target: Moreau, A. (2019). Greedy pruning of ensembles. Invented Journal, 1, 1-10.
Okafor, B. (2020). Proper scores for classifiers. Invented Journal, 2, 11-20.
